newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria car bomb kills seven, wounds 48.
newsitem.headline: Algeria car bomb kills seven, wounds 48.

text.p: A huge car bomb exploded in central Algiers on Tuesday afternoon, killing seven people and wounding 48, several of whom were in a critical condition, security forces said in a statement.

An official source told Reuters by telephone that the security forces said the bomb went off at 14.15 (1315 GMT) near the main university faculty. The authorities have blamed previous bomb attacks on Moslem fundamentalists.
According to a police source the blast rocked the area near the end of Algiers's main shopping street, Rue Didouche Mourad, blowing out windows and setting cars and one bus ablaze.
One eyewitness said: "There were an awful lot of wounded. I saw a fireman picking up an arm from the ground."
Another witness, a crying student, said: "Not only have we had the strike (of university teachers) but now we have bombs."
Heavily armed security forces, initially police but later soldiers, sealed off the area.
One resident of the area said they had refused to let him in even to return home. "There is possibly a second bomb in there," he said security force members told him.
At least five burnt-out cars and the twisted wreck of the bus could be seen before the area was sealed off, witnesses said.
All the windows in the La Brass cafe, a popular haunt of university students and staff, were shattered, with shards of glass lying deep on the pavement.
University students are due to return to class on January 13.
One witness said the car bomb was placed in a Honda accord.
Algiers has been the target of numerous bomb attacks blamed by the authorities on Moslem fundamentalists. Two car bombs in Algiers late in December killed at least 18 people.
The latest blast occurred amid a spate of rebel raids on villages in which at least 38 people were killed within a 24-hour period last week.
The violence flared as Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia said in a speech at the weekend that his government had crushed the Islamist guerrillas.

He said that what he called the remnants of the "terrorists" had been forced to turn to attacks on isolated areas because they had been thwarted in what he called "secure areas" -- Algeria's towns and cities.

About 60,000 people have been killed, including more than 1,400 in bomb attacks, in Algeria since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.

The worst bombing in Algiers was in 1995 when Moslem rebels slammed a car laden with explosives into the main police station in Colonel Amirouche street, killing more than 40 people and wounding more than 300. Diplomats at the time said a more accurate figure was over 100 dead.
